_about: Alkene addition rows (docs/ch8-10-app-gaps.md, 'Design: an addition engine that never guesses'). Checked in order, first match wins, like rules.json. when: sub (alkene | alkane | epoxide), act (the reagent's `add` role in reagents.json), x (halogen of HX/X2), heat, light, peroxide, water. then: intermediate (cation | halonium | radical | concerted | surface | ozonide | none), regio (markovnikov | anti-markovnikov | none), stereo (syn | anti | none), shifts, adds { more, less } (what ends up on the more / less substituted C=C carbon), stereospecific (Y | N), build (markovnikov | radical | ozonolysis | halonium | hydroboration | hydrogenation | epoxidation | epoxideOpen; missing = the product builder isn't written yet, so the row says addition_not_yet but still reports its classification), session (when the builder lands), template (viewer, S4), reasons. notCovered rows stop with that reason. Rows may carry tags: course | disagree.

faces._about: Facial selectivity probe and 3D placement (faces.js). probeHeight/cutoff in Å; ratio = more ÷ less hindered face needed for tier 1 (computed); agreeWindow in kcal/mol (every conformer this close to the lowest must agree); bond = Å from the carbon for each new atom (by atomic number). Calibration (S2, 2026-11-14, seeds 42/1/7/99): 2a 1.74, 2m 1.69, 2j 1.47–1.70 → tier 1; 2i 1.27–1.33 and 3-methylcyclohexene (a textbook mixture) 1.23–1.28 overlap within seed noise, so the doc's 1.3 was raised to 1.4: 2i falls to tier 2 with the same answer, 3-methylcyclohexene stays a mixture. 2c 1.05, Q4 1.04–1.26, 4-Me/4-tBu-cyclohexene and 1-Me-4-tBu-cyclohexene ≤ 1.07, norbornene 1.00 (textbook: exo, so the probe can't see that one: tier 3), camphene 1.02.

reasons.not_sn_e_reagent: This isn’t an SN/E reagent (it has an O–O, X–X or H–H bond, or boron: an oxidant, halogen, H₂ or borane), so no SN/E role is estimated for it. If it’s in the reagent list, type its name instead.
reasons.addition_not_yet: This addition (Ch 8) isn’t built yet, so no product is shown. The card still says what kind of addition it is.
reasons.radical_not_yet: This is an alkane with a halogen and light: radical halogenation (Ch 10) isn’t covered yet.
reasons.addition_alkene_type: A C=C carbon here carries O, N, a halogen, or is conjugated with C=O or C≡N. Those change where H⁺ adds, and the addition engine doesn’t cover them yet.
reasons.conjugated_diene: Conjugated diene: 1,2- vs 1,4-addition isn’t covered yet.
reasons.several_alkenes: This molecule has more than one C=C, and one equivalent of reagent could add to either. The app doesn’t pick one.
reasons.alkyne_not_covered: Additions to C≡C (alkynes) aren’t covered yet.
reasons.workup_alone: This is the second half of a two-part step (it follows BH₃ or O₃). Type both, e.g. “1) O₃ 2) DMS”.
reasons.needs_workup: BH₃ and O₃ are two-part steps: the first part alone gives an organoborane or an ozonide, which the course never stops at. Add the second part (BH₃ → H₂O₂/HO⁻; O₃ → DMS or Zn/HOAc).
reasons.needs_catalyst: H₂ alone doesn’t add to a C=C: it needs a metal catalyst (Pd/C, Pt, PtO₂ or Ni).
reasons.oxidative_workup: O₃ with an oxidative workup (H₂O₂) turns aldehydes into carboxylic acids. That isn’t covered yet; reductive workup (DMS or Zn/HOAc) is.
reasons.hydration_vs_dehydration: Acid with heat and no water on an alkene: hydration is an equilibrium, and heat without water pushes it back toward the alkene (dehydration). Add water (H₂SO₄ in H₂O) for hydration.
reasons.allylic_needs_nbs: Br₂/Cl₂ with an alkene still adds across the C=C, even with light. Substituting an allylic H needs NBS (low Br₂ concentration), which isn’t covered yet.
reasons.alkene_also_reacts: The C=C can also add this reagent; only the substitution/elimination at the leaving group is shown.
reasons.markovnikov: Markovnikov: H⁺ adds to the C=C carbon that leaves the more stable carbocation (more carbons on C⁺, or allylic/benzylic). The nucleophile then bonds to C⁺.
reasons.cation_shifts: A carbocation can rearrange: a 1,2-hydride or methyl shift happens only if it gives a more stable cation.
reasons.markovnikov_tie: Both ends of the C=C give equally stable carbocations, so both products form (competing). The app doesn’t pick one.
reasons.hydration: Acid-catalysed hydration: H⁺ adds (Markovnikov), water bonds to C⁺, then loses H⁺ to give the alcohol.
reasons.acid_water_assumed: Acid without heat on an alkene is read as hydration in water (the usual conditions), so OH ends up on the more substituted carbon.
reasons.hbr_radical: HBr with peroxides (ROOR) goes by a radical chain: Br• adds to the C=C end that leaves the more stable radical, so Br ends up on the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov).
reasons.radical_no_shift: Radicals don’t do 1,2-shifts here, so there’s no rearrangement.
reasons.only_hbr_radical: Only HBr adds by the radical chain. With HCl or HI one step of the chain is uphill, so peroxides change nothing: it’s an ordinary Markovnikov addition.
reasons.halonium_no_shift: Br₂/Cl₂ form a three-membered bridged halonium ion: no free carbocation, so no shifts, and the nucleophile opens it from the back (anti).
reasons.halohydrin_regio: Water opens the halonium ion at the more substituted carbon, which carries more δ+.
reasons.concerted_no_shift: Concerted: all bonds form at once, there’s no intermediate, so nothing can rearrange.
reasons.hydroboration_regio: B goes to the less substituted carbon (less crowded); H₂O₂/HO⁻ then swaps B for OH with retention, so OH ends up on the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov), syn with the new H.
reasons.hydrogenation_surface: H atoms are delivered from the metal surface to one face of the C=C (syn).
reasons.ozonolysis_cut: Ozonolysis cuts every C=C: each alkene carbon becomes a C=O. A ring C=C gives one chain with two carbonyls; =CH₂ leaves as formaldehyde.
reasons.reductive_workup: Reductive workup (DMS or Zn/HOAc) keeps aldehydes as aldehydes.
reasons.racemic_flat: The new stereocentre forms at a flat carbocation or radical, so both faces react equally: a racemic mixture (±).
reasons.mixture_flat: The new stereocentre forms at a flat carbocation or radical next to another stereocentre: a mixture of diastereomers.
reasons.no_3d: The 3D shape for this molecule couldn’t be built, so the app can’t place the new atoms on a face. No product is shown rather than a guess.
reasons.boron_tie: Both C=C carbons carry the same number of carbons, so B can go to either: both alcohols form (competing).
reasons.face_tier1: Face: the reagent adds to the less hindered face of the C=C, computed from the 3D shape (every low-energy shape agrees).
reasons.face_tier2: Face (course rule): the 3D shape shows only a small difference between the faces, so the textbook rule is used: the reagent adds anti to the group on the neighbouring stereocentre. Expect some of the other isomer.
reasons.face_tier3: Face: the two faces of this C=C are different, but neither the 3D shape nor a course rule decides between them. Both products are shown (mixture of diastereomers: facial selectivity not covered).
reasons.opening_undecided: The halide can open the bridged ion at either carbon, and here that gives different stereoisomers. The 3D shape doesn’t decide which, so both are shown.
reasons.alkene_geometry_unknown: The C=C is drawn without a set E/Z geometry, and the product’s stereochemistry depends on it. Products are shown without wedges: draw the E or Z alkene to see the stereoisomer.
reasons.substrate_stereo_undefined: A stereocentre in the starting material is drawn without wedges, so only the relative configuration (cis/trans to it) is meaningful.
reasons.racemic_faces: The starting material is achiral, so both faces react equally: the product forms as a racemic mixture (±). One enantiomer is drawn; the other forms equally.
reasons.meso_product: The product has a mirror plane: it is meso (achiral), so there is no racemate.
reasons.single_isomer: The starting material is a single enantiomer, so this product forms as a single stereoisomer.
reasons.relative_only: Only the relative configuration is shown (the starting material’s stereocentre isn’t drawn with wedges).
reasons.epoxide_sn2: Epoxide opening is SN2: the nucleophile attacks a ring carbon from the back, opposite the ring O, so that carbon inverts (anti opening). A cis epoxide gives a trans product.
reasons.epoxide_acid_regio: In acid, the O is protonated first and the C–O bond to the more substituted carbon is weaker, so water attacks there when one carbon is 3°.
reasons.epoxide_base_regio: With a strong nucleophile (HO⁻) and no acid, it attacks the less hindered (less substituted) carbon.
reasons.epoxide_tie: Both epoxide carbons are equally substituted, so the nucleophile attacks either: all products are shown.
reasons.epoxide_acid_mixed: In acid, a 1° vs 2° epoxide carbon isn’t clear-cut (sterics and δ+ pull opposite ways), so both products are shown.
reasons.achiral_cis_trans: The product is achiral: its only stereochemistry is cis/trans on the ring, so it forms as one cis/trans isomer with no racemate.
reasons.stereospecific_meaning: Stereospecific (textbook meaning): stereoisomeric starting alkenes give different stereoisomeric products. For example, (E)-but-2-ene + Br₂ gives meso-2,3-dibromobutane, while (Z)-but-2-ene gives the racemate.
reasons.stereospecific_course: Your course key calls this addition stereospecific because the mechanism fixes how the groups add (anti, through the bridged ion), even when there is no E/Z pair to compare (Q8C).
